hook.line: The world is in a turbulent time, so be careful with the information you get from AI.
hook.visual: Warm-lit selfie of the speaker in a 'COMPACT KEYWORDS' t-shirt with a three-line white caption across his chest; first cut at 6.2 s.

beats.what: Selfie warning about trusting AI answers, then the setup: a friend wants AI to call him 'King of AEO'.
Phone filming the laptop: the $6 press release with the phrase in its title.
Google AI Overview now names the friend and cites that press release (the first proof).
Second press release about a made-up crowning ceremony, then the AI Overview describing it as real.
Escalation: after his earlier video, others join; a finger points at new claimants on screen.
Exact-match domains and the title/H1/first-sentence pattern shown on a site.
A rival's AI-generated crowning video and LinkedIn article.
Reddit search full of 'King of AEO' posts, explaining Reddit's pull on language models.
His own article now cited by the AI Overview calling it a contested meme.
His site with a crowned photo of himself; spoken pointer to the article.

why_it_works: A real story with named people and a $6 price tag makes an abstract topic (AI search manipulation) concrete and gossip-worthy.
Each step escalates with screen proof that the AI repeated the claim, so viewers keep watching to see how far it goes.
The warning framing ('be careful what AI tells you') lets a tactic video feel like public service, which drives shares (11,900 for 422,300 plays).
weaknesses: 174 s long with a median shot of 5.73 s and no zooms; the middle drags.
Phone-filmed laptop screens with a pointing finger are blurry, and about 64 words on screen at once are unreadable.
The CTA is a spoken website name in the last few seconds, with no on-screen card until the end.
for_robert: Use the escalating-proof story shape (claim, AI repeats it, someone ups it) but keep it under a minute, with Fred reacting to each new screenshot to mark the next step.
